Numbers are where most candidates lose me, and they lose me in one of two ways. Some give me no numbers at all. They tell me the company grew a lot, and I have no idea whether a lot means ten percent or ten times. Others give me so many numbers that I stop listening after the third one. Here is what works. Give me one headline figure, and round it. Nobody needs to hear four hundred and eighty-four point six million. Just under four hundred and eighty-five million is perfect, and so is almost half a billion. Then give me one comparison, so that I know whether the number is big or small. And then stop. If I want the breakdown, I will ask for it. The candidates I remember are not the ones with the most numbers. They are the ones who told me what one number meant.

The worst number I ever had to present was a cost overrun of twenty-two percent on a hospital project. The board saw that figure on the first slide, and the room went quiet. I had two choices. I could hide it in the breakdown, or I could put it into perspective. I chose the second. I explained that almost three quarters of the overrun came from one decision, a change in the ventilation system that the client asked for after the pandemic. Without that change, the overrun was in the region of six percent, well under the industry average. Then I showed them the trend. Overruns on our projects had peaked three years earlier and had been falling steadily since then. The board approved the next project that same afternoon. The number did not change. What changed was the comparison they had in their heads.
